data.title: Blatnohrad – Pribina’s seat in Pannonia
data.excerpt: In 2009 a sherd bearing a Glagolitic inscription was dug up near Zalavár — the oldest one surviving in the Slavic world. It cannot be ruled out that it was written by Methodius himself, who stayed here for half a year.
data.metaTitle: Blatnohrad – Pribina’s seat and the oldest Glagolitic text
data.metaDescription: Pribina’s and Koceľ’s seat near Zalavár, where in 2009 a sherd with a Glagolitic inscription was found — the oldest in the Slavic world.

children.text: Blatnohrad (Mosapurc in German), today Zalavár about 9 km south-west of Lake Balaton, was the seat of Pribina in the Principality of Blatnohrad after he had been forced to leave his original domain in the Nitra region. Under his successor Koceľ it was the centre of the learning of the Slavs. In 2009 a great stir was caused by the find of a sherd on which a legible fragment of a text written in the Glagolitic script survives.

On the inscription of the sherd, which comes from a jug or a bottle, the letters “i” and “o” (called iže and on) can clearly be seen, that is, “io” together. It may be, for instance, part of some name. For the time being it is not possible to determine exactly which language is involved. Scholars from countries that use the Cyrillic script may help to clarify this. This find is of exceptional value for Slavic culture. It is, after all, the oldest surviving lettering in the Glagolitic script. It cannot even be ruled out that it was written by Methodius himself, or by one of his pupils, because in 866–867 they were staying at Blatnohrad.

Blatnohrad was built on a natural elevation, or rather on an island among the marshes, and consisted of three larger parts: a fortified seigneurial stronghold, a centrally placed ecclesiastical part, where a pilgrimage church also stood, and a residential quarter, called suburbium in Latin.

children.text: Most of the buildings — among them also the archbishop’s residence, the remains of which were uncovered in 2000–2007 — were built of wood. The pottery fragment with the Glagolitic inscription was found in the deepest part of a three-metre-deep ditch which once separated the former stronghold from the ecclesiastical part. On the basis of the layers above it, this find cannot be dated any later than about the year 870. The Glagolitic inscriptions known so far come from the 10th–11th centuries, which is why the Blatnohrad find is remarkable.

Many Slovaks, and especially those who travel through the Hungarian Balaton onwards to Croatia, have no idea that they are passing through a region once ruled by the Nitran prince Pribina and his son Koceľ. About 2 km from the town of Nagykanizsa there is a junction where one can turn off towards the spa town of Zalakaros. After roughly fifteen kilometres, once you have passed through the villages of Garabonc, Nagyrada and Zalaszabar, you will notice a brown signpost in Hungarian and English. It will direct you to a monument — a sculptural group of Saints Cyril and Methodius — at the village of Zalavár. It stands on the site that was once called Blatnohrad, Mosapurch or Mosaburg. It was built as a fortified seat in the middle of the marshy terrain of the river Sala (Zala) by Prince Pribina.

Blatnohrad was the centre of his principality, which until the arrival of the Old Hungarians formed an extensive territory: in the south it reached as far as the river Drava, in the east to the river Danube, in the north to the town of Veszprém, and in the west it extended into present-day Styria, Carinthia and Slovenia. It included the present-day towns of Veszprém and Szombathely in Hungary, Leibnitz in Styria and Ptuj in Slovenia.
Pribina’s asylum

After the demise of Samo’s Empire (623–659) the Western Slavs formed several tribal principalities. At the beginning of the 9th century the most important and strongest of them were the Principality of Nitra and the Principality of Moravia. The princes often fought among themselves and attempted to enlarge their own territories. In 833 Mojmír I, the ruler of Moravia, succeeded in conquering the Principality of Nitra (which comprised the territory of the whole of present-day Slovakia and part of the territory between the Danube and the Tisza) and annexing it to his own principality. By this union he created the stronger realm of Great Moravia. Its centre was in Moravia (probably Velehrad, or rather Uherské Hradiště) and Nitra became merely the seat of the heir to the throne.

children.text: The Nitran prince Pribina, his son Koceľ and a retinue of magnates (Chotemír, Vlčina, Žeško, Trebič, Čestislav, Zemiň) managed to flee to the Franks. They took refuge with Ratbod, the governor of the frontier Eastern and Carinthian March, with whom Pribina traded (the well-known ancient Amber and Salt Routes passed through the Principality of Nitra) and with whom he also had family ties — he took as his wife Ratbod’s daughter, a Christian, in whose honour he built the first Christian church in Nitra in 828.

After his flight Pribina entered the service of the Frankish Empire. First, however, he had to be baptised and instructed in the Christian faith. In 833 he was baptised in the church of St Martin at Traismauer (Ratbod’s seat), in present-day Austria. To commemorate this event, a memorial plaque dedicated to “the Slovak Prince Pribina” was unveiled on this church in May 1990. The ceremonial Slovak holy mass was celebrated by the Salzburg archbishop Karl Berg, by Cardinal Ján Ch. Korec, bishop of Nitra, and by Archbishop Ján Sokol, the Slovak metropolitan.

children.text: Later, however, Pribina came into conflict with Ratbod and took refuge with the Bulgarians in the Bulgarian Empire, where he sought an outlet for his ruling abilities and allies for restoring his rule in the Principality of Nitra. When he had no success there, he went to Slavonia (Croatia), to Prince Ratimir, who was fighting Ratbod. In 838 Ratbod defeated Ratimir, when at the decisive moment he was abandoned by Pribina, who later made his peace with Ratbod… This happened at a time when Pribina realised that there was no possibility of restoring his rule in Nitra. Ratbod introduced Pribina to the Frankish king Louis, called the German. In 840–846 the latter granted him in fief the territory of Lower Pannonia by Lake Blatno (Balaton), which he carved out of the extensive Carinthian March.

children.text: On this territory, which in 847 is already mentioned as Pribina’s own principality, he gathered population, spread Christianity, built new churches (the first in 850 dedicated to the Virgin Mary, and another 12 before Pribina’s death) and monasteries from which learning spread. The
Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum

records that Pribina and his people also built strategic centres and economic, cultural and military structures. They cultivated the fields, exploited the riches of the forests, and introduced the breeding of horses, cattle and sheep. At the end of Pribina’s life (861) the principality was an important neighbour of the Slavic lands — Great Moravia, Croatia and Bulgaria.
Koceľ’s work

After Pribina’s death (he died in a battle with the Moravians, who were fighting against King Louis — they supported the rebellion of his son Carloman) the rule was taken over by his son Koceľ (830–876). He continued his father’s work. He supported the spread of Slavic culture and the work of Saints Cyril and Methodius, who in 867, during their mission to Great Moravia, also stopped at Blatnohrad for half a year. They devoted themselves to teaching more than fifty selected pupils, and Koceľ himself also learned to read books written in the Old Church Slavonic Glagolitic script. When Cyril died in 869, Koceľ sent a letter to Pope Hadrian II in which he asked him to send Methodius as a teacher to the Principality of Blatnohrad. In the middle of 869 the pope sent a joint bull to Rastislav, Svatopluk and Koceľ concerning the sending of Methodius as a teacher to their lands. In the summer of 869 the papal curia, at Koceľ’s instigation, appointed Methodius metropolitan of Pannonia and Great Moravia.

According to research, in 870–871 Koceľ was the only Slavic ruler who informed the pope of Methodius’s imprisonment. In 873, despite Frankish threats (Frankish priests and rulers were opposed to the strengthening of the ecclesiastical and political independence of Great Moravia and of the Principality of Blatnohrad), he came in person to collect the released Methodius.
The wealth of the magnates

Prince Koceľ continued his father’s legacy in the building of the cultural and economic centres of the principality as well. The basis of the economy was agricultural production and organised nomadic pastoralism. Settlements below the strongholds (suburbia) were built, where craftsmen were concentrated. Ore was mined, metal was worked, charcoal was burnt. Potters, smiths and basket-makers excelled.

Surviving records also speak of the wealth of some of the magnates at Koceľ’s court. Unzat, for example, had extensive territories in Vas county (Železná župa), in the area of the Zala and by Lake Neusiedl. He built several settlements and many hamlets, and also a church that was consecrated in 865 by the archbishop of Salzburg. The magnate Zemin built the Iron Castle (Vasvár). Žilic, whose seat was in Somogy county, owned thousands of hectares of forest. To this day the place is still called Zselicség or Zseliczerdő.

Prince Koceľ died in 876 or 877, as the end of Great Moravia was approaching. It is not known whether he left a male descendant behind him, since in 880 the administration of the Principality of Blatnohrad was entrusted to the Croat Braslav. The Frankish emperor Arnulf relinquished the Principality of Blatnohrad (Transdanubia) to the arriving Hungarians, who came into the area in 900–901. Stephen, the first Hungarian king, founded a monastery in honour of Saint Hadrian at Blatnohrad in 1019. From the end of the 11th century Pribina’s former stronghold was a county castle and the seat of Zala county. In the 16th century (after reconstruction work) it was incorporated into the system of anti-Ottoman frontier fortresses. In 1702 it was blown up so that it would not fall into the hands of the Kuruc rebels.

On its site the West Transdanubian Water Management Directorate (Nyugatdunántúli Vízügyi Igazgatóság) built the House of the Little Balaton, which was opened in 2000 in order to make the water conservation system and the aquatic world of the Little Balaton accessible to tourists. The construction of this house brought to a close the archaeological excavation that had lasted several years (it began in 1946) and during which it proved possible to find the foundations of Pribina’s stronghold, measuring 150 × 200 metres, the suburbium, the stronghold enclosure, the foundations of the churches dedicated to the Virgin Mary and to St Hadrian, an extensive cemetery, and a settlement 5–6 kilometres from the stronghold, where finds of craft workshops are expected. Many finds and relics from the 9th century are kept in the depositories of the Balaton Museum in Keszthely.

children.text: A large part of the find spots has been backfilled (most recently in 2001), or has fallen victim to nationalist politics, which probably does not wish to admit that the territory of Transdanubia was inhabited not only by the Avars and the Franks but by Slavs as well. Even the only visible relic of the remains of the foundations of Pribina’s stronghold, which is near the House of the Little Balaton, is neither marked nor named. They lie in the middle of great marshes. With my eyes I touch the remains of the walls. The poet Ján Kollár must have seen them too; in 1842 he drew the foundations of one of Pribina’s churches, when they were still visible at that time.

In 798 Charlemagne entrusted the Salzburg archbishop Arno with the Christianisation of Pannonia. He charged the archbishopric of Salzburg with the task of going to this region to build and consecrate churches, to send parish priests there and to educate the people through preaching. After the fall of the Avar Empire, Zalavár, the seat of Prince Pribina, formed the centre of missionary activity reaching as far as Pécs (Päťkostolie). During this period more than thirty churches were built. Three of them at Zalavár: one in honour of the Virgin Mary, the second in honour of Saint John the Baptist and the third in honour of the martyr Saint Hadrian. The disputes that arose after the activity of the Slavic apostle Methodius in 866–870 had a harmful effect on this missionary work, which came to an end at the beginning of the 10th century.

children.text: The ruins of the basilica

The era of Pribina and Koceľ is indirectly recalled by the remains of the basilica on the island of Récéskút. On the site of what was probably the original altar stands a metal cross bearing a plaque with the following text: “This place was consecrated in the year 850”. Nothing more.
